summary: Describes how to include a key identifier in a CMS enveloped data structure so the content encryption key can be reused for further encrypted packets.

eli5.summary: It puts a label on a key so you can use it again without making a new one every time.

questions: how to reuse a content encryption key
why reverse the bytes of the cek
subtitle: A small trick for reusing one message's encryption key to protect the next message, without another expensive key exchange.

tldr.problem: Setting up an encrypted CMS message with asymmetric (public-key) cryptography is relatively expensive, so sending many messages that way is wasteful.
tldr.mechanism: The first message carries a key identifier (CEKReference) for its content-encryption key. The key-encryption key of the next message is derived from that key by reversing its bytes, or by PBKDF2 when the algorithms differ.
tldr.outcome: Peers that talk often can save work, but the RFC defines only a building block, not a protocol, and it adds no authentication or replay protection.

facts.label: Default KEK derivation
facts.value: Byte reversal of the previous CEK

today: RFC 3185 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself stresses that it is a building block that each using context must complete.

sections.title: The Idea of Reusing a Key
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 2630) defines EnvelopedData, which encrypts data using either symmetric or asymmetric key management. Establishing a key with asymmetric methods is relatively expensive, so in some environments it is attractive to reuse a shared content-encryption key (CEK) for later messages.

The basic idea is to take the CEK of one message (MSG1) and use it to derive the key-encryption key (KEK) of a later message (MSG2). MSG1 carries a reference value for its CEK, and MSG2 uses that same value as its KEKIdentifier. The CEK from MSG1 is called the referenced CEK.
sections.eli5: The first message's secret key gets a name tag. The second message uses that name tag to say which old key it is built from, so nobody has to start from scratch.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
The RFC aims at more efficient selective field confidentiality between communicating peers. Two cases are named: a client sending several fields to a server in one transaction, with the referenced CEK encrypting each field separately, and two servers that talk very frequently and use the scheme purely for efficiency.

It is explicitly not for every case. It does not define a protocol, only a trick that needs further specification in each context, and that specification is REQUIRED to define what originators and recipients do when a referenced CEK has been lost. It is not suitable for general group key management. A cryptographic API that completely hides key bits from the CMS layer will probably prevent reuse, and the content and key-encryption algorithms must have compatible key values and strengths. For example, a 40 bit cipher in MSG1 and a key-encryption algorithm needing 168 bits of keying material in MSG2 SHOULD NOT be combined.

If an implementation already supports group key management, this scheme adds no value.
sections.eli5: This trick is a handy shortcut for people who chat often, not a full set of rules. It only works if both locks use keys of about the same size and strength.

sections.title: Referencing and Deriving the Key
sections.content:
To reference the CEK, MSG1 MUST include an unprotectedAttrs attribute of type id-aa-CEKReference with a single value, an OCTET STRING. MSG2's KEK is derived by reversing the bytes of MSG1's CEK. The reversal exists so that an attacker who knows some plaintext and its ciphertext (encrypted with MSG1's CEK) cannot directly use that ciphertext as MSG2's KEK. The attribute can appear with any RecipientInfo choice (ktri, kari or kekri), and MSG2 can carry its own CEKReference, so the referenced CEK can be rolled with every message.

An originator MAY also include a CEKMaxDecrypts attribute, an INTEGER of at least 1 and at most 2^31, giving the maximum number of messages (excluding MSG1) that will use the referenced CEK. It MUST only be sent together with a CEKReference. Recipients SHOULD keep the key identifier and CEK while fewer than that many messages have arrived, and SHOULD delete it after a locally configured period. If the attribute is absent, both sides behave as if the value were one, so each CEK is reused once, as the KEK of the next message.
sections.eli5: The new key is the old key written backwards. Writing it backwards means a sneaky person who knows part of the old message cannot just copy a piece of it to get the next key.

sections.title: Different CEK and KEK Algorithms
sections.content:
When the content-encryption algorithm of MSG1 and the key-encryption algorithm of MSG2 differ, for example because they need different key lengths, byte reversal is not enough. Implementations MAY support a generic alternative: run the PBKDF2 function from PKCS#5 (RFC 2898) with MSG1's CEK as input instead of a password. The output is MSG2's KEK.

The parameters travel in a KEKDerivationAlgorithm attribute holding kekAlg, the algorithm identifier for MSG2's key encryption, and the PBKDF2 parameters. The salt MUST use the specified choice, the originator picks the iterationCount, keyLength is set by kekAlg and MUST be present, and the prf field MUST be omitted so the default HMAC-SHA1 applies. The RFC notes that altering kekAlg would only enable a denial-of-service attack, so it needs no protection.
sections.eli5: If the two locks need keys of different sizes, a blender is used to turn the old key into a new key of the right size. The sender tells the receiver which blender settings were used.

sections.title: Conformance Rules
sections.content:
The specification applies only to messages with a CEKReference attribute. The other attributes SHOULD be ignored unless the message contains a valid CEKReference, either new or an existing recognized one. Recipients treat CEKMaxDecrypts as a hint, but the originator MUST honor it.

The KEKDerivationAlgorithm attribute is optional to implement, but when MSG1's content-encryption algorithm differs from MSG2's key-encryption algorithm it MUST be present. An implementation that recognizes it without supporting it SHOULD ignore it. Ignoring attributes leads to decryption failures, so CMS implementations SHOULD be able to tell the calling application the particular reason for the failure.
sections.eli5: If the helper labels are missing or not understood, the message simply cannot be opened, and the program should say why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption is not authentication. Recipients MUST NOT assume that knowing a CEKReference value proves who sent the message, and MUST NOT assume that a correct CEKReference means the message was not replayed or inserted.

A large maxDecrypts value could make a recipient store referenced CEKs for a long time, or the originator might never send the promised messages. Recipients SHOULD drop CEKs when the value is too large or the CEK is held too long, according to local configuration.

If MSG1 went to a set S1 of users and MSG2 goes to only some of them, every user in S1 can still decrypt MSG2, since MSG2's KEK comes only from MSG1's CEK. Implementers should also be careful if MSG[n].KEK is used to derive MSG[n].CEK, because that could unexpectedly lead to a fixed key. Byte reversal was chosen over bit reversal because bit reversal would put parity bits of DES-based keys into keying positions.
sections.eli5: A matching label does not prove who wrote the note. Anyone who got the first message can open the later ones too, even if they were not meant for them.

viz.caption: THE THREE ATTRIBUTES DEFINED BY RFC 3185

items.label: CEKReference
items.desc: OCTET STRING key identifier for the CEK of this message, used later as a KEKIdentifier.

items.label: CEKMaxDecrypts
items.desc: INTEGER hint: the maximum number of later messages that will use the referenced CEK.

items.label: KEKDerivationAlgorithm
items.desc: Names the key-encryption algorithm and PBKDF2 parameters when byte reversal cannot be used.
